transcript.text: "Hey." Amelia settles near you, not too close. "Day one. Everyone's pretending they're fine. ...Can we talk? Just talk — like people used to."
"I’m listening."
"What do you make of all this? Really."
"The world's ended. We're what's left."
"Bleak. Probably true. I keep looking for the part where it's not."
"Yeah?"
Their voice loosens. The guardedness thins.
"Yeah?"
"I think we're an experiment someone forgot to label. And the unlabeled part is what scares me — it means nobody's coming to check the results."
"Wait — what were we talking about?"
"Still on what you make of all this."
"Yeah?"
"What's something from your old life that's actually useful here?"
"Patience. Sounds dumb. But waiting — really waiting, without fidgeting — that's a superpower now."
"Not dumb at all. The people who can't wait are the ones who make mistakes. You're an asset."
"Yeah?"
"Being a fisherman taught me to read people fast — who's lying, who's scared, who needs a job. Turns out that's a survival skill. Who knew."
"Yeah?"
"I should get back to it."
"Good talk. I feel like I know you a little better now."
"About who you don't trust — Is there someone here you don't trust? Be honest."
"Yeah. I'm not saying who. But yeah."
Their eyes flick, just for a second, toward the fire. "Noted. I'll watch too."
"Yeah?"
A small chill settles between you. They're choosing words more carefully.
"Yeah?"
"I don't distrust anyone exactly — I just haven't finished trusting most of them yet. There's a difference. A slow one."
"Wait — what were we talking about?"
"Still on who you don't trust."
"Wait — what were we talking about?"
"Like I said — we're still on who you don't trust."
"Yeah?"
"What do you miss most? From before."
"A real hot meal."
"God. Yes. I dream about soup. Actual soup, with a spoon."
"Yeah?"
"Here's the thing: Hot showers. Not the big things — the small, stupid, perfect things. Columbus, Ohio in the morning, coffee going, nobody trying to kill me. I miss being bored."
"Yeah?"
"Anyway — I should get going."
"Good talk. I feel like I know you a little better now."
They nod, already turning away.
"What's something you're good at that nobody here knows about?"
"I'm better with my hands than people expect. You'll see."
"Fine — Noted. Filing that under 'extremely useful.' The village needs that."
"Teach me something from the wild."
"There's more, but that's for another fire."
"Go on."
"I can do trapping. Not well — well enough that nobody's died from it yet. That's my whole résumé now: nobody's died from it yet."
"Wait — what were we talking about?"
"Still on what you're good at."
"Go on."
"Where are you from — originally? Before all this."
"I'm from Columbus, Ohio."
Nods slowly. "Columbus, Ohio. I'll remember that. Everybody's from somewhere that isn't here."
"Go on."
"Me? Columbus, Ohio. I still dream in its weather — rain on a tin roof, that specific smell. I wake up here and for a second I'm furious at the sky for the swap."
"Go on."
"Okay, that's my quota of socializing."
They glance at the fire, then back. The quiet doesn't seem to bother them.
"Good talk. I feel like I know you a little better now."
"About that question — What's your first memory? Like, ever. The earliest thing. Simple as that."
"A kitchen. Morning light. I must've been three."
"Three. That's young. The brain keeps what it needs, I guess."
"Yeah?"
They pull back half a step — not leaving, just... further.
"Yeah?"
"Right, so — Mine's Columbus, Ohio, I think — heat on pavement, someone's hand huge around mine. Or I invented it. First memories are half real and half the story you needed."
"Wait — what were we talking about?"
"Still on your first memory. That matters to me."
"Yeah?"
"...Hi. Sorry. I'm not good at the talking-to-strangers part."
"Neither am I, honestly."
Something eases in their shoulders. "Oh. Okay. That's... that's fine, then."
"Yeah?"
"Strangers are just people you haven't disappointed yet. That's what my mother said. Terrible advice, but it got me through parties. I mean it."
"What do you think it means?"
"What do you think is actually going on here?"
"That deer wasn't standing right. Too still. Real deer flick their ears — this one didn't move a muscle for ten minutes."
"I'm listening."
Something in them almost softens — then doesn't. Not yet.
"I'm listening."
"Alright. Catch you later."
The silence stretches a beat too long. They study their hands.
"Good talk. I feel like I know you a little better now."
"Right. Well." That's the whole goodbye.
"What are you hoping for? Not the big stuff. The small thing. That is all."
"A full night's sleep. Just one. Where I don't wake up listening."
"God, yes. That's the dream now. Eight hours of not being afraid."
"Go on."
"A full night's sleep. Not safety, not answers — just eight hours where nothing needs me. That's my whole theology now. Seen worse."
"Go on."
"Walk with me? I want another pair of eyes on something."
"All right. Let's go."
